article_title: Determinants of Students' Success: The Role of Advanced Placement and Dual Enrollment Programs
citation: Cecilia Speroni. (2011). Determinants of Students' Success: The Role of Advanced Placement and Dual Enrollment Programs. National Center for Postsecondary Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Offer dual enrollment on college campuses rather than exclusively on the high school campus to support college access
description: The study's findings support locating dual enrollment courses on college campuses: only students who took "dual enrollment classes on college campuses" showed higher college-going and bachelor's degree attainment, while students who took "these classes exclusively on the high school campus showed no statistically significant gains." The article's summary presents the campus setting as the operative difference between the participating groups.
requirements: Dual enrollment courses must be taken on a college campus for the positive impacts to be expected, per the study's contrast between campus settings.
constraints: The evidence is observational, comparing participants with similar non-participants rather than randomly assigned students; no significant gains were found for the high-school-campus setting.
target_learning_goals: college enrollment
bachelor's degree attainment
examples: The study tracked all of Florida's 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 high school seniors and compared dual enrollment participants by course location.
key_sources: Cecilia Speroni. (2011). Determinants of Students' Success: The Role of Advanced Placement and Dual Enrollment Programs. National Center for Postsecondary Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/determinants-of-students-success-the-role-of-advanced-placement-and-dual-enrollment-programs

article_title: Measuring What Matters: Considerations for Measuring the Implementation of High-Quality Instructional Materials in Mathematics
citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Curriculum enactment as a translation process from official curriculum through teacher-intended curriculum to enacted curriculum
description: The report conceptualizes instructional materials as "resources that specify intended teacher and student interactions with mathematics" and frames implementation as a chain of translations: official curriculum, teacher-intended curriculum, and enacted curriculum. Figure 1 depicts a dynamic system with official and operational sections, reciprocal feedback from student outcomes to enacted and intended curricula, and external factors shaping all stages. Teachers add, modify, and omit curricular elements based on attitudes, beliefs, and goals, so the enacted curriculum is a personalized, flexible version of the intended one.
requirements: Understanding enactment requires data from multiple actors in the translation chain, including curriculum developers, district leaders, teachers, and students
constraints: The report notes teachers must make professional decisions in complex, dynamic environments, so intended interactions seldom go as planned
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning through standards-aligned core curriculum implementation
examples: The study's four research questions and instruments are organized around capturing each translation stage, from developer intent to student experience
key_sources: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681340

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Design offline-capable educational AI as an equity strategy for low-connectivity settings, and evaluate it under local bandwidth, device, and cost constraints
description: Offline-first deployment reframed as equity architecture rather than a degraded compromise: designing for local inference removes the connectivity assumption that excludes rural learners, extending the system's reach. The article argues educational AI for low-connectivity settings should be evaluated "not only for response quality under ideal conditions, but also for whether they remain usable under the bandwidth, device, and cost constraints that characterize the communities they are intended to serve." Quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning make local inference on consumer hardware feasible, with sustainability co-benefits.
requirements: Local inference feasibility depends on quantization techniques and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., quantized 7-billion-parameter models)
Evaluation frameworks must test usability under the target community's bandwidth, device, and cost constraints
constraints: The article frames this as a prioritization choice among users rather than claiming offline systems match cloud capability on response quality
target_learners: Rural learners in low-connectivity environments in Bangladesh and comparable contexts
target_learning_goals: Access to AI tutoring, debugging assistance, and native-language explanations without reliable connectivity
examples: The article notes local inference on a quantized 7-billion-parameter model consumes a fraction of the energy of routing each query through a remote cloud API, material at school computer-lab scale
key_sources: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Offer pedagogical training early in university teaching careers, including short online formats
description: Because conceptions form lenses for interpreting teaching and are hard to change once entrenched, the article recommends low-threshold, timely support before and at the start of teaching. Its stated conclusion is that “pedagogical training should be offered already at the early stages of teaching careers”, since even short online programmes changed interpretations “especially when participants are not very experienced in teaching”. This addresses the barrier that traditional lengthy face-to-face courses exclude doctoral students and new faculty who lack teaching duties.
requirements: Short online formats with guided study so that staff not currently teaching can participate
constraints: The article reports doubts about the efficacy of programmes lasting less than six months to one year, and that more experienced teachers are more likely to be reluctant to change their conceptions or practices
target_learners: New university faculty in their first years of teaching
target_learning_goals: Adopting learning-facilitation conceptions of teaching before habits of teaching as taught become entrenched
examples: The UNIPS courses were five weeks long, one ECTS credit each, and open to doctoral students without teaching duties, who completed tasks such as planning an imaginary course.
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: Unraveling the influence of domain knowledge during simulation-based inquiry learning
citation: Ard W. Lazonder, Pascal Wilhelm, Emiel van Lieburg. (2009). Unraveling the influence of domain knowledge during simulation-based inquiry learning. Instr Sci, 37, 437-451. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9055-8
title: Offer learners some information about the relations between variables in a domain to support efficient and successful inquiry learning
description: The article recommends that when relations in a domain cannot be inferred from the meaning of variables, learners should be given some information on those relations. It argues such knowledge "can bootstrap students' inquiry practices" and "can safeguard students from the adverse consequences of their quest for meaning", since learners readily induce rationales that are prone to error. This balances the inquisitory nature of learning against the need to overcome learning obstacles.
requirements: Learners are engaged in inquiry learning in a domain whose variable relations they cannot readily infer from variable meanings alone
constraints: The article notes the choice of what information to present depends upon the characteristics of the learner and domain at hand
The study was not designed to advocate tasks with unknown variables or relations; how students can be supported on a just-in-time basis is an open question for future research
target_learners: College freshmen in simulation-based inquiry tasks; the article suggests science students who have difficulty understanding material or did not prepare for class may face similar conditions
target_learning_goals: Discovering relationships between variables in an unfamiliar domain through hypothesis generation and experimentation
examples: In the experiment, only the concrete task, whose variables allowed inference of relations, produced more efficient (lower exploratory percentage) and more successful inquiry than the intermediate task
key_sources: Ard W. Lazonder, Pascal Wilhelm, Emiel van Lieburg. (2009). Unraveling the influence of domain knowledge during simulation-based inquiry learning. Instr Sci, 37, 437-451. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9055-8

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Offloading regulation: a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization
description: The article proposes offloading regulation as the competence to govern the cognitive partition between learner and GenAI, positioned as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components. It comprises partition discernment (judging what may be offloaded without erosion), calibrated monitoring of whether understanding is developing, disciplinary verification of AI outputs, and re-internalization of offloaded content through re-deriving, self-explaining, or unaided attempts. It is enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners' goals and motivation.
requirements: Metacognitive monitoring whose signal tracks actual understanding rather than fluency-based ease
Disciplinary competence sufficient to evaluate AI outputs, which novices may lack
constraints: Conditioned by learners' goals and motivation; the review notes learners who know which strategies work often do not use them
target_learners: STEM learners in K–12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: Governing the learner–AI division of cognitive labor so that offloading supports rather than supplants durable learning
examples: Student C treats an AI-generated model as a worked example, checks the fit against residuals, explains why a linear model fails, and later re-derives the doubling time unaided
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths?
citation: Tamar Kricheli-Katz and Tali Regev. (2021). The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths? npj Science of Learning 6:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00087-7
title: Grant test takers the choice of being addressed in the feminine or the masculine in exams
description: Because address form causally affects performance in gendered languages, the article recommends that learners be allowed to choose their form of address. As the authors put it, "to improve women’s performance, women and men should be granted the right to choose whether they wish to be addressed in the feminine or in the masculine in exams." This follows from their finding that feminine address helps women but can modestly hurt men in some contexts, so a blanket switch is not optimal for everyone.
requirements: Assessment instructions written in a gendered language must offer both masculine and feminine address forms to test takers.
constraints: Effects of feminine address on men were negative in some contexts, although smaller than the effects on women and marginally significant; effects were established in an online, individually taken test setting, not a classroom.
target_learners: Adult and adolescent test takers in gendered-language settings
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement test performance
examples: In the main experiment, a representative sample of Hebrew-speaking adults took an SAT-type maths test online, randomly addressed in the feminine or the masculine; women addressed in the feminine scored higher and the gender gap shrank.
key_sources: Tamar Kricheli-Katz and Tali Regev. (2021). The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths? npj Science of Learning 6:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00087-7

article_title: Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency
citation: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9
title: Use free, publicly available, unmodified large-scale speech models to scale oral reading fluency assessment in lower-resource contexts
description: Because top open-source models now transcribe children's oral reading accurately without fine-tuning, ORF assessment can be automated where one-on-one assessment is too costly. The authors argue the combination of "accurate transcription, ability to handle diverse accents, and production of reliable ORF scores" could enhance literacy assessment where regular individualized assessment has been blocked by resource constraints, enabling more frequent progress monitoring.
requirements: Recordings of students reading passages aloud, plus the original story text and audio duration to compute WCPM
Model transcripts must be evaluated against the original text to capture student reading errors, not normalized away
constraints: Findings rest on only two specific ASR models, a relatively small sample from two datasets (Ghana and the United States), and English-only assessment
Automated WCPM does not match expert scores exactly; the authors frame ORF as a formative or diagnostic measure where small measurement errors are unlikely to hurt practical use
target_learners: Beginning and intermediate readers in lower-resource, linguistically diverse education contexts, particularly the Global South
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment and monitoring of oral reading fluency
examples: The study used Whisper V2 and wav2vec 2.0 out-of-the-box on classroom recordings from Ghana and validated automated WCPM against expert human raters on 165 assessments
key_sources: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9

article_title: Mind the Teachers! The Impact of Mindfulness Training on Self-Regulation and Classroom Performance in a Sample of German School Teachers
citation: Rupprecht, S., Paulus, P. & Walach, H. (2017). Mind the teachers! The impact of mindfulness training on self-regulation and classroom performance in a sample of German school teachers. European Journal of Educational Research, 6(4), 565-581. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.6.4.565
title: Offer mindfulness training to interested teachers as a professional-development option for building self-regulation capacity
description: The article concludes that mindfulness training "together with diligent home practice of mindfulness can help teachers to improve their self -regulation capacity, their well -being and their self -efficacy." It recommends implementing such trainings "as a potential instrument for teacher training, at least for those teachers that find such a training appealing." The training requires substantial time commitment and voluntary interest.
requirements: Teachers must be willing to commit to daily home practice (participants averaged 29.7 minutes of formal practice per day on 80% of designated days)
Training should be offered voluntarily to interested teachers rather than as a mandatory prerequisite
constraints: Teachers in the study cautioned the course is "not for everyone" and should not be made a prerequisite
Effects demonstrated only in a self-selected, mostly female, non-randomized sample
target_learning_goals: improve self-regulation capacity
improve teacher wellbeing and self-efficacy
reduce occupational strain
examples: A 5-week adapted MBSR course (four 2.5-hour evenings and two 8-hour days, 26 hours total) delivered at a teacher training institution with sessions credited toward compulsory continuing-education hours
key_sources: Rupprecht, S., Paulus, P. & Walach, H. (2017). Mind the teachers! The impact of mindfulness training on self-regulation and classroom performance in a sample of German school teachers. European Journal of Educational Research, 6(4), 565-581. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.6.4.565

article_title: A Meta Analysis on Effective Conditions to Offer Animation Based Teaching Style
citation: Kaushal, R. K., & Panda, S. N. (2019). A Meta Analysis on Effective Conditions to Offer Animation Based Teaching Style. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 16(1), 129-153. https://mjli.uum.edu.my
title: Offer animation-based teaching only to learners who already have sufficient prior knowledge of the domain
description: Because the meta-analysis found a positive mean effect for high prior knowledge learners (0.49) and a negative effect for low prior knowledge learners (-0.16), the article concludes that "prior knowledge is a crucial factor while offering animations and it should only be offered to the HPK students". Educators should treat prior knowledge of the domain/topic as the most important factor when deciding whether to teach through animations, since LPK students generally were unable to perform well with them.
requirements: Learners' prior knowledge level must be assessed before selecting animation-based teaching
constraints: The finding is based on published experiments aggregated across domains; the authors recommend evaluating the effect according to specific domain in the future
target_learners: high prior knowledge learners in secondary school, high school, and university
target_learning_goals: improving learning outcomes when teaching topics that require changes over time and space
examples: The study statistically compared weighted mean effect sizes of HPK (0.49) and LPK (-0.16) groups taught through animated versus non-animated environments
key_sources: Kaushal, R. K., & Panda, S. N. (2019). A Meta Analysis on Effective Conditions to Offer Animation Based Teaching Style. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 16(1), 129-153. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1219792

article_title: Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine.
citation: Delirrooyfard Ali, Sayyah Mehdi, Ahmady Soleiman, Kohan Noushin. (2026). Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09094-x
title: An online flipped classroom clinical reasoning course for emergency medicine clerkship, designed via a modified ADDIE model
description: An 8-week clinical reasoning course for emergency medicine clerkship students, developed using "a modified version of the ADDIE instructional design model, specifically adapted by Eltahir for virtual learning environments". It comprised asynchronous pre-class content (short videos under 30 minutes via WhatsApp and an LMS, with mandatory formative MCQ tests), synchronous 60-minute small-group case-based Zoom discussions using a think-aloud format, and bedside application sessions. Evaluation used Kirkpatrick levels 1 and 2 (satisfaction and OSCE-based learning outcomes).
requirements: Participants required a smartphone with WhatsApp to engage with asynchronous electronic content
Mandatory formative tests via the LMS after each video module to ensure engagement before synchronous sessions
constraints: Excluded students with prior formal exposure to flipped classroom models or clinical reasoning workshops
Excluded students missing more than 20% of online pre-class activities or more than one bedside think-aloud session
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students during emergency medicine clerkship
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and diagnostic logic in high-acuity emergency presentations
History taking and differential diagnosis prioritization
key_sources: Delirrooyfard Ali, Sayyah Mehdi, Ahmady Soleiman, Kohan Noushin. (2026). Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09094-x

article_title: Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine.
citation: Delirrooyfard Ali, Sayyah Mehdi, Ahmady Soleiman, Kohan Noushin. (2026). Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09094-x
title: Use a structured online flipped classroom design to develop clinical reasoning during clinical clerkships
description: The article supports integrating online flipped classroom instruction into clinical clerkships as a structured alternative to informal bedside teaching. The design pairs asynchronous pre-class content with synchronous think-aloud case discussion, so that, as the authors put it, "in-person bedside sessions were exclusively dedicated to the application of these concepts through real patient cases". The authors frame this as preliminary, proof-of-concept evidence for integrating blended learning into emergency medicine curricula.
requirements: Asynchronous pre-class content must be completed before synchronous sessions, enforced via mandatory formative tests
Synchronous sessions require faculty facilitators able to provide targeted probing questions and immediate corrective feedback
constraints: The article reports only pilot/feasibility evidence from a single-group quasi-experimental design without a control group; definitive effectiveness, generalizability and scalability require future controlled trials
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students during clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Diagnostic logic in high-acuity care
examples: The article implemented an 8-week course with short instructional videos via WhatsApp and an LMS, followed by 60-minute synchronous small-group think-aloud sessions via Zoom during the emergency medicine clerkship
key_sources: Delirrooyfard Ali, Sayyah Mehdi, Ahmady Soleiman, Kohan Noushin. (2026). Enhancing diagnostic logic in high-acuity care: evidence from an online flipped classroom intervention in emergency medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09094-x

article_title: Comparing structured note-taking and multiple-choice question writing as learning strategies among physiotherapy students.
citation: Wrzesińska Magdalena A., Rakoczy Jarosław, Binder-Olibrowska Katarzyna W., Kostyła Magdalena, Allott Vincent E.S., Harris Samuel R.L., Walsh Jason L., Handa Ashok, Harris Benjamin H.L. (2025). Comparing structured note-taking and multiple-choice question writing as learning strategies among physiotherapy students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08272-7
title: Offer students both note-taking and MCQ creation options to cater to diverse learning preferences
description: The article concludes that educators should provide both post-seminar assignment formats rather than choosing one, since exam outcomes were equivalent but preferences diverged sharply. It states: "Educators should consider offering both NT and MCQ creation to students, thereby catering to diverse learning preferences and enhancing the overall educational experience." Allowing choice may improve engagement, though this was not tested in the trial.
requirements: Instructors must be able to review and grade both submission types against predefined criteria, as faculty did in the trial on a pass/fail basis
constraints: The equivalence finding comes from a single institution, a single psychology course with non-clinical content, and first-year physiotherapy students only
target_learning_goals: consolidation of seminar content in preparation for summative examinations
examples: In the trial, all students completed both assignment types in crossover arms; the recommendation to offer choice is for future implementation and study
key_sources: Wrzesińska Magdalena A., Rakoczy Jarosław, Binder-Olibrowska Katarzyna W., Kostyła Magdalena, Allott Vincent E.S., Harris Samuel R.L., Walsh Jason L., Handa Ashok, Harris Benjamin H.L. (2025). Comparing structured note-taking and multiple-choice question writing as learning strategies among physiotherapy students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08272-7

article_title: Exploring the integration of OFST and IPE in cross-regional physiology teaching-a novel approach.
citation: Wang Ting-Huai, Xu Xiao-Dan, Long Zhi-Yuan, Cao Ying-Nan, Lai Ning-Yi, Ma Yong-Hong, Tan Xiao-Qiu, Xin Min, Jiang Jin-Yan, Yang Da-Ya. (2025). Exploring the integration of OFST and IPE in cross-regional physiology teaching-a novel approach. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07412-3
title: Online Four-Step Teaching (OFST) model grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy
description: OFST is a structured, team-based, task-driven online teaching model adapted from the traditional Four-Step Teaching of encouraging and sharing. It sequences four steps — teacher guidance, self-regulated learning, team learning and practice, and experience sharing — mapped onto Bloom's six hierarchical cognitive levels so that "The six levels of the taxonomy are integrated within the four steps of OFST, ensuring a scaffolded learning approach". Steps 1–2 build lower-order skills and autonomy; Steps 3–4 integrate peer-assisted learning, interprofessional collaboration, case-based problem-solving, peer feedback, and instructor moderation aligned with evaluate and create.
requirements: Online platform supporting synchronous teaching (the study used Ding Talk Online Classroom)
Trained teachers familiar with the OFST model and its implementation
Interprofessional group composition with at least two different disciplines per group
constraints: In the reported implementation the model was applied to a single complex physiology topic (coronary circulation) with limited classroom time
target_learners: undergraduate health-professions students across medicine, nursing, pharmacy, medical imaging and related majors
target_learning_goals: foundational physiology knowledge
clinical application and problem-solving
self-regulated learning
teamwork and interprofessional collaboration
examples: In this study the four steps were delivered on coronary circulation: guided teaching with checkpoints, 2–3 days of self-regulated learning followed by Quiz 1, an interprofessional myocardial infarction case study followed by Quiz 2, and slide-based group presentations with peer feedback and awards
key_sources: Wang Ting-Huai, Xu Xiao-Dan, Long Zhi-Yuan, Cao Ying-Nan, Lai Ning-Yi, Ma Yong-Hong, Tan Xiao-Qiu, Xin Min, Jiang Jin-Yan, Yang Da-Ya. (2025). Exploring the integration of OFST and IPE in cross-regional physiology teaching-a novel approach. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07412-3

article_title: Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities.
citation: Supriya K., Bang Christofer, Ebie Jessica, Pagliarulo Christopher, Tucker Derek, Villegas Kaela, Wright Christian, Brownell Sara. (2024). Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11440740/
title: Offer optional grade-improvement opportunities during formal class time to reduce scheduling barriers and broaden participation
description: The article argues that optional grade-improvement opportunities such as exam retakes should be scheduled during formal class time because many students balance coursework with jobs and caregiving. Comparing courses, "a much larger proportion of students retook exams in Course 2, when exams were offered during class time or online compared with Courses 1 and 3, where exams were offered outside of class time". The authors argue this would eliminate scheduling barriers to participation.
requirements: The course must include formal class time that can be allocated to the optional assessment opportunity
constraints: Offering retakes during class time still is not enough to overcome barriers for students with limited time, because effective retaking involves preparing outside of class
In Course 2, some disparities in participation and benefits persisted even with in-class/online retakes
target_learners: undergraduate students in large introductory STEM courses, including students who work jobs or have caregiving responsibilities
target_learning_goals: equitable participation in optional grade-improvement opportunities
reduced scheduling barriers to assessment retakes
examples: Course 2 offered retakes during class time or online and had higher participation than Courses 1 and 3, where retakes were outside of class time
Students who worked a job were more likely to agree they would have preferred exam retakes during class time
key_sources: Supriya K., Bang Christofer, Ebie Jessica, Pagliarulo Christopher, Tucker Derek, Villegas Kaela, Wright Christian, Brownell Sara. (2024). Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11440740/
